text: Here is the problem. The only consciousness anyone observes directly is their own. For everyone and everything else, we infer it, mostly from what people say. So scientists look for signatures in the brain, and check them against people who can report what they experienced. Then they ask how far those signatures can be trusted.

text: The first tool is the perturbational complexity index, or P C I. Researchers send a brief magnetic pulse into the cortex, record the brain's echo with E E G, and measure how complex that echo is. In a 2013 study by Casali, Massimini and colleagues, awake people and dreamers gave rich, varied echoes. Deep sleep and anesthesia gave simpler ones.

text: In 2016, the same group set a cutoff using 150 people who could report whether they were conscious. In that group, it separated conscious from unconscious perfectly. They then applied it to 81 patients who could not communicate. About 95 percent of the minimally conscious patients scored above the cutoff, and so did 9 of 43 patients diagnosed as vegetative. That suggests some of them may be conscious, but unable to show it.

text: Be careful what this means. P C I measures how rich the brain's response is. It does not say what is being experienced. And it was calibrated on people who could talk. It is a strong clue about a level of consciousness, not a window into anyone's mind.

text: A second tool asks patients to imagine something. In 2006, Adrian Owen's team asked a patient diagnosed as vegetative to imagine playing tennis, or walking around her home. Her brain scan lit up the expected regions, just like healthy volunteers. In 2024, a study of 353 patients found that 60 of the 241 who showed no response to commands at the bedside still did this kind of task, about one in four.

text: Behind these tools sit rival theories. Global workspace theory says information becomes conscious when it is broadcast across the brain, an event called ignition, with the front of the brain playing a key role. Integrated information theory says consciousness depends on how a system's parts causally affect each other, and points to the back of the cortex. These theories predict different brain activity. So they can be tested against each other.

text: That is what a large team did. The Cogitate consortium, with proponents of both theories agreeing on the predictions in advance, studied 256 people viewing images, using three kinds of brain recording. The result, published in Nature in April 2025: both theories got some support, and both were challenged. Integrated information theory expected sustained synchronization in the back of the cortex, and it was lacking. Workspace theory expected ignition when an image disappeared, and mostly it was not there.

Others, including the philosopher David Chalmers, called that label disproportionate. A new test in monkeys and mice was described in a published protocol in 2026. We found no results yet.

text: Now animals. In 1970, Gordon Gallup marked chimpanzees with red dye and gave them a mirror. The chimps touched the marks, which suggests they recognized themselves. The monkeys he tested did not. Since then, magpies in 2008 and, far more disputed, a small fish called the cleaner wrasse in 2019 have been reported to pass. Critics note the test checks one thing, self-recognition. An animal that fails is not shown to lack experience.

text: So for animals, researchers weigh many kinds of evidence. In April 2024, scientists and philosophers released the New York Declaration on Animal Consciousness. It says there is strong support for consciousness in mammals and birds, and a realistic possibility of it in all vertebrates and many invertebrates, including octopuses, crabs and insects. That is a statement about probability, not a measurement.

text: This is why behavior alone cannot settle the question. Two systems can act the same way for different reasons. A chatbot trained on human writing can talk fluently about feelings, because humans do. So its words are weak evidence either way. In 2023, Patrick Butlin, Robert Long and colleagues took another route. They took leading theories, listed what each says a conscious system would need, and checked AI systems against those indicators.

text: Their analysis suggested that no current AI systems are conscious. It also suggested there are no obvious technical barriers to building systems that satisfy the indicators. That is a judgment relative to certain theories, and the theories disagree. Workspace-style views treat consciousness as a kind of information processing, so a machine with the right design could count. Integrated information theory looks at physical causal structure, so software behavior alone would not settle it.

text: So what is established? Brain measures can track levels of consciousness in people who can report, and some unresponsive patients show hidden awareness. What is disputed? Which theory is right, and how testable they are. What is open? Whether any test can say if a fish, an octopus or a machine has experience. Right now, none can.
